want.now.why: SOV: object खासी and infinitive सीखना come first, then the door चाहता, then हूँ carrying present tense last. चाहता is masculine because the learner is male.

want.past.why: Past is just the final auxiliary swapped, हूँ to था; the door चाहता itself does not change shape at all.

want.neg.why: नहीं sits right before the door, and in speech the हूँ drops after नहीं, so चाहता ends the sentence alone with no tense carrier.

want.q.why: क्या at the front makes a yes/no question; nothing inverts. Informal तुम takes the plural-looking चाहते हो even for one friend.

decline.now.why: English can't splits into नहीं + सकता and the हूँ drops after नहीं. After क्योंकि the doer is dative मुझे; for a one-off, spoken Hindi often says just काम करना है.

decline.past.why: Both doors go perfective with no था: सका and पड़ा carry the past by themselves. आना is intransitive, so मैं takes no ने.

decline.fut.why: Unlike English, CAN has a real future: सकूँगा with the -ऊँगा ending, and पड़ेगा does the same for HAVE-TO. Spoken Hindi says नहीं आ पाऊँगा just as often.

decline.although.why: Hindi fronts the concession: हालाँकि clause first, then फिर भी (even so) opens the main clause, a pair like अगर...तो. Clause order flips versus English.

like.now.why: The liker is dative मुझे and कॉफ़ी is the grammatical subject; है agrees with कॉफ़ी, not with me, so nothing here would change for a female speaker.

like.neg.why: Here नहीं slips in after the door, between पसंद and है, unlike चाहता where it goes before. Casual speech drops the है: पसंद नहीं.

like.she.why: Only the dative pronoun changes, मुझे to उसे; पसंद है is untouched and shows no gender since it agrees with कॉफ़ी. उसे is he or she alike.

like.q.why: क्या fronted, informal dative तुम्हें; the verb stays है because कॉफ़ी is the subject, so nothing in the sentence agrees with you at all.

go.habit.why: Time रोज़ comes before place and the verb group जाता हूँ closes. बाज़ार takes no postposition after जाना, so 'to the market' is a single bare word.

go.prog.why: Progressive is bare stem जा plus रहा (masculine, agreeing with me) plus हूँ: two carriers after the verb where English has one 'am' before it.

go.past.why: गया is the perfective participle standing alone as the past, masculine to match मैं. जाना is intransitive so no ने; कल means yesterday and tomorrow.

go.fut.why: One synthetic future जाऊँगा fuses verb and tense where English needs 'will'. For a fixed plan people say कल बाज़ार जा रहा हूँ instead.

go.neg.why: नहीं goes right before the whole verb group जा रहा हूँ; in speech the final हूँ often drops after नहीं (मैं बाज़ार नहीं जा रहा).

live.now.why: No perfect tense: plain present progressive रह रहा हूँ plus से on the duration does the work of 'have been living'. Duration comes before place.

live.past.why: Finished period: bare दो साल with no से (or दो साल तक), and this रहा is the perfective of रहना 'stayed', not the progressive marker.

live.fut.why: Hindi flips it: 'to me, living here, three years will happen'. Dative मुझे, participle रहते हुए, and the tense sits on हो जाएँगे, agreeing with तीन साल.

live.q.why: The question word कब से (since when) stays in place just before the verb instead of fronting; रहे हो is the तुम form, plural-looking for one friend.

if.real.why: Possession is मेरे पास 'with me', and the if-clause verb goes perfective (वक़्त हुआ, 'if time happened'). तो opens the result and has no English word.

if.unreal.why: Unreal: the bare habitual participle in both halves, होता ... जाता, with no auxiliary anywhere; English 'would' has no separate word. जाता is masculine.

if.past.why: The if-clause is identical to the unreal one; only the result shifts to perfective plus होता (गया होता) to mark the missed past. No ने: जाना is intransitive.
